cls: Selective serotonin 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonist (triptan); acute anti-migraine agent
pharm: A second-generation triptan that selectively activates 5-HT1B/1D receptors on intracranial blood vessels and trigeminal sensory nerves, producing cranial vasoconstriction and inhibition of pro-inflammatory neuropeptide release to abort an acute migraine attack. Compared with sumatriptan it has a slower onset but longer half-life and lower headache-recurrence rate.
quick: 1 mg or 2.5 mg orally at onset; may repeat once after 4 h; max 5 mg/24 h
May be taken with or without food
Limited data; animal fetal harm - use only if clearly needed
No human milk data; caution / consider avoiding
Mild-moderate: start 1 mg, max 2.5 mg/24 h; CrCl <15 contraindicated
Mild-moderate (Child-Pugh A/B): max 2.5 mg/24 h; severe (C) contraindicated
No specific interaction; alcohol may itself trigger migraine
Blood pressure, cardiovascular risk, headache frequency / overuse
summary: Naratriptan is an oral triptan for the acute treatment of migraine with or without aura in adults. It is not for migraine prophylaxis or for cluster headache. Because it constricts coronary and other arteries, it is contraindicated in patients with ischemic heart disease, coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal angina), prior stroke/TIA, peripheral or ischemic bowel disease, uncontrolled hypertension, Wolff-Parkinson-White or other accessory-pathway arrhythmias, and hemiplegic or basilar migraine. It must not be used within 24 hours of an ergotamine-containing drug or another triptan, and serotonin syndrome can occur with serotonergic drugs. The dose is limited in renal and hepatic impairment, and it is contraindicated when creatinine clearance is below 15 mL/min or in severe hepatic impairment.
indications: Acute treatment of migraine with or without aura in adults
NOT indicated for prevention/prophylaxis of migraine
NOT indicated for cluster headache or for hemiplegic or basilar migraine

dosage.d: 1 mg or 2.5 mg as a single dose at onset of headache
dosage.t: Once at onset; may repeat after >=4 h
dosage.n: Maximum 5 mg in any 24-hour period; 2.5 mg is the higher recommended single dose

dosage.d: A second dose may be taken if the headache returns, no sooner than 4 hours after the first
dosage.n: Do NOT take a second dose if the first dose gave no relief - benefit unproven; reassess diagnosis

dosage.d: Start 1 mg; maximum 2.5 mg in 24 hours
dosage.t: Once; repeat after >=4 h if needed
dosage.n: Clearance reduced ~50% (CrCl 18-39 mL/min); half-life prolonged to ~11 h

dosage.d: Start 1 mg; maximum 2.5 mg in 24 hours
dosage.t: Once; repeat after >=4 h if needed

dosage.d: Treating more than 4 attacks per 30 days has not been established as safe

admin: Take a single tablet as early as possible after migraine onset; efficacy is similar whether taken early or late but early treatment is generally preferred
Swallow the tablet whole with water; may be taken with or without food
Wait at least 4 hours before any repeat dose, and do not exceed 5 mg in 24 hours
Do not take if an ergotamine/ergot-type drug or another triptan has been used within the past 24 hours
Confirm a clear migraine diagnosis and screen for cardiovascular risk before the first dose; consider giving the first dose under medical observation in patients with cardiac risk factors
moa: Naratriptan is a selective agonist at vascular 5-HT1B and neuronal 5-HT1D serotonin receptor subtypes, with little affinity for other 5-HT, adrenergic, dopaminergic, muscarinic, or benzodiazepine receptors. Two actions are thought to underlie its anti-migraine effect: (1) agonism at 5-HT1B receptors on intracranial (including meningeal/dural) blood vessels causes vasoconstriction of the cranial vessels that are pathologically dilated during a migraine; and (2) agonism at 5-HT1D receptors on peripheral trigeminal sensory nerve terminals inhibits the release of pro-inflammatory and vasoactive neuropeptides (e.g., CGRP) and dampens nociceptive transmission within the trigeminovascular system. The same 5-HT1B-mediated vasoconstriction acts on coronary and other systemic arteries, which underlies the drug's cardiovascular contraindications.

absolute: Ischemic coronary artery disease (angina pectoris, prior myocardial infarction, documented silent ischemia)
Coronary artery vasospasm, including Prinzmetal (variant) angina
History of stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA)
Peripheral vascular disease or ischemic bowel disease
Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome or arrhythmias associated with other cardiac accessory conduction pathway disorders
Use within 24 hours of an ergotamine-containing or ergot-type medication, or of another 5-HT1 agonist (triptan)
Concurrent use of (or within 2 weeks of stopping) a monoamine oxidase inhibitor - risk of serotonin syndrome
Known hypersensitivity to naratriptan or any component
relative: Cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, obesity, strong family history, postmenopausal women, men >40 y) - assess and consider first-dose monitoring
Concurrent serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs) - serotonin syndrome risk
Mild-to-moderate renal or hepatic impairment - reduce dose
monitor: Cardiac symptoms - chest/throat/jaw/neck tightness, pressure, or pain after dosing
Signs of serotonin syndrome when combined with serotonergic agents
Headache frequency and analgesic/triptan use to detect medication overuse

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Based on animal data, naratriptan may cause fetal harm (embryolethality and developmental abnormalities were seen at clinically relevant exposures). Pregnancy-registry data are insufficient for a definitive risk assessment. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: It is not known whether naratriptan is present in human milk; it is excreted in the milk of lactating animals. Because of the potential for adverse effects in a breastfed infant, exercise caution; consider avoiding breastfeeding or limiting infant exposure (e.g., withholding feeds for a period after a dose) based on the drug's half-life.
renal: Naratriptan is partly eliminated by the kidneys (about 50% excreted unchanged in urine). In mild-to-moderate renal impairment, clearance is reduced (roughly halved at CrCl 18-39 mL/min) and the half-life is prolonged (to ~11 hours); start at 1 mg and do not exceed 2.5 mg in 24 hours. It is contraindicated in severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance below 15 mL/min).
hepatic: Hepatic metabolism (via cytochrome P450) contributes to clearance, so exposure increases in liver disease. In mild-to-moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh grade A or B), start at 1 mg and do not exceed 2.5 mg in 24 hours. It is contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh grade C).

major: Ergotamine / ergot-type drugs (dihydroergotamine, methysergide) - additive prolonged vasospasm; do not use within 24 hours of each other
Other 5-HT1 agonists (other triptans) - additive vasospastic effects; separate by at least 24 hours
MAO inhibitors - serotonin syndrome risk; contraindicated
SSRIs / SNRIs and other serotonergic agents - serotonin syndrome (agitation, hyperthermia, clonus, autonomic instability)
moderate: Other vasoconstrictors - additive blood-pressure and vascular effects
St. John's wort - additive serotonergic risk
minor: Oral contraceptives and tobacco use modestly alter naratriptan clearance but no dose change is required
interactions.food: Food does not meaningfully affect absorption; may be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: No specific pharmacologic interaction with naratriptan, but alcohol can itself precipitate migraine and may worsen drowsiness/dizziness.

common: Throat and neck tightness or discomfort
Sensations of pain, pressure, heaviness or warmth
serious: Coronary vasospasm, angina, myocardial ischemia or infarction
rare: Hypersensitivity reactions including angioedema and anaphylaxis
emergency: Chest pain, tightness, or pressure suggesting cardiac ischemia
Signs of stroke (sudden weakness, speech or visual changes)
Serotonin syndrome (high fever, agitation, clonus, rigidity)

monitoring: Blood pressure before and during therapy
Cardiovascular status and symptoms after dosing, especially with risk factors
Headache frequency and triptan/analgesic use (medication-overuse headache)
Signs of serotonin syndrome when used with serotonergic drugs
Renal and hepatic function in patients with impairment
counsel: Take this medicine as soon as your migraine headache starts; it treats attacks but does not prevent them
If your headache comes back, you may take one more dose after at least 4 hours, but never take more than 5 mg in one day
Do not take a second dose if the first dose did not help at all - call your doctor instead
Do not use within 24 hours of another migraine triptan or any ergot/ergotamine medicine
Stop and seek emergency care if you get chest, throat, jaw, or arm tightness or pain, severe headache, or trouble speaking or moving
Tell your doctor about heart disease, high blood pressure, stroke, or all other medicines, especially antidepressants
Using migraine medicines on more than about 10 days a month can cause more frequent headaches
pk: Relief begins ~1-2 h; slower onset than sumatriptan
Tmax ~2-3 h (3-4 h during a migraine attack); oral bioavailability ~70%
~6 h (prolonged to ~11 h in moderate renal impairment)
Long for a triptan; lower 24-h headache-recurrence rate
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); excursions 15-30 C permitted
pearls: Slowest-onset but longest-acting oral triptan - favored when headache recurrence is the main problem rather than speed of relief

Screen every patient for cardiovascular disease/risk - it is contraindicated in ischemic heart disease, coronary vasospasm, stroke/TIA, PVD, ischemic bowel, uncontrolled HTN, and WPW/accessory-pathway arrhythmias
Never within 24 hours of an ergot drug or another triptan; never with an MAOI
Do NOT redose if the first dose was completely ineffective - reassess the diagnosis
Contraindicated in hemiplegic and basilar (brainstem-aura) migraine
Dose-cap and contraindication thresholds: max 2.5 mg/24 h in mild-moderate renal/hepatic impairment; contraindicated if CrCl <15 or Child-Pugh C
Watch for serotonin syndrome when combined with SSRIs/SNRIs
missed: Naratriptan is taken only as needed for an acute migraine attack, not on a fixed schedule, so there is no missed dose. Take a dose when a migraine begins, respect the 4-hour interval before any repeat dose, and never exceed 5 mg in 24 hours.
overdose: Overdose may cause exaggerated effects including marked hypertension and other serious cardiovascular effects (coronary or peripheral vasospasm, arrhythmias), as well as dizziness, fatigue, and CNS depression. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive with continuous cardiovascular monitoring for at least 24 hours (the half-life is ~6 hours) and treatment of hypertension and ischemia as needed; the effect of dialysis is unknown.
